result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of Elis, describing a ruined Roman Emperors' colonnade and the temples of Aphrodite near the market-place. He explains why the Eleans alone honour Pluto and describes the temple of Fortune, the shrine of Sosipolis and a statue called Satrapes.

scenes.title: Market-place and Aphrodite's temples
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes a ruined colonnade for the Roman Emperors and the temple and grove of Aphrodite, with statues by Phidias and Scopas.

scenes.title: The temple of Pluto
scenes.summary: Pausanias explains that the Eleans honour Pluto because he helped Pylos against Hercules, citing Homer, and opens his temple yearly.
scenes.stakes: Pluto and Pylos face Hercules' attack; Pluto is wounded by his arrow.

scenes.title: Fortune, Sosipolis and Satrapes
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the temple of Fortune, the shrine of the boy Sosipolis and the statue of Poseidon called Satrapes.

alias_notes.explanation: Elis calls its statue of Poseidon Satrapes, a name learnt from Patrae and also a surname of Corybas.
Epithet of the Scopas statue on the he-goat.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias openly declines to explain the tortoise and goat symbolism.

analysis.text: Pausanias links local cult practices to myth and Homer to explain unusual worship, such as Pluto's yearly-opened temple.
The section shows Roman imperial cult entering Greek towns and the fusion of local gods with foreign names like Satrapes.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says Pluto's Elean temple is opened only once a year, and only the priest may enter.

language_notes.text: The Corcyræan Portico was a colonnade in Elis, apparently named for spoils or a dedication from Corcyra (Corfu).
"Celestial" translates Urania, the heavenly Aphrodite, in contrast to the Pandemian ("of all the people") Aphrodite of the grove.
Hercules' campaign against Elis and Pylos was a legendary war in which he punished King Augeas and others; Athene commonly aids him.
Quoted from Iliad 5: Hercules wounded Hades at Pylos. Ægis-bearing Zeus is the translator's rendering of Jupiter/Zeus as father of Hercules.
The horn of Amalthea is the cornucopia, the horn of plenty, named for the nurse of Zeus in myth.
Corybas was a divine attendant figure linked with the Great Mother's cult; the identification is Pausanias' own claim.

context_notes.text: Phidias was the celebrated Athenian sculptor who also made the great gold-and-ivory Zeus at Olympia.
Scopas of Paros was a famous fourth-century BC sculptor.
Pluto is the god of the dead, called Hades by the Greeks, so his cult was rare and gloomy.
Sosipolis, "saviour of the city," was an Elean child-god who, in legend, appeared as a serpent to aid the Eleans in battle.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias openly declines to explain the symbols, addressing readers directly and showing his cautious, reticent attitude toward religious mysteries.
Pausanias defends the Elean tradition by comparing it with Poseidon helping the Greeks at Troy, using Homer as his authority.
The yearly opening of Pluto's temple symbolises that death's realm is entered only once, by all men, in the end.
